title: Valencia, Silver Slipper and Gulf Coast gigs
summary: Hug lists later jobs including the Valencia cabaret and the Silver Slipper with Sidney Arodin, and a homesick week on the Gulf Coast.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: I just want to get one more thing on the biography before we go on. After you started with this group at the Fern, was it? Yeah. Did you do mostly after that single work? I've known you always as a single since I was first a jazz fan. Did you have any other gigs that you think were especially worthy of note, either with a group or as a single, that were important to you as you developed in your career?

Not as a single, Charlie, because I worked with groups there. I went from the Fern dance hall over to a little nightclub or cabaret, they call it in those days, called the Valencia, where the Hilton Inn is supposed to go up today on Bourbon Street. And I worked there with a little three-piece group with Chink Morton's son, who played banjo, and Eddie Miller, who played alto sax in those days. And we had a little three-piece outfit. And, well, from there I went to various places. I don't know if I can get them just in order, but I worked at the Silver Slipper, which later, in later years, became known as the Dream Room, and now the Father's Mustache. But in those days, the Silver Slipper nightclub was really one of the real swing places in the city. And I worked there with a very fine musician by the name of Sidney Arden. Sidney Arden, you know, wrote Upper Lazy River. And, of course, Hoagie Carmichael collaborated with Sidney on this tune. Well, naturally, I mean, very few people ever refer to the tune as Sidney's. They always say Hoagie's tune. Well, of course, actually, and not to take any credit away from Hoagie, the tune originally was, from what I can understand, and I quote other musicians, that Sidney had this tune for quite a while, but it was under a different title. I won't quote the title because the title was not very appropriate. Okay. Did you do much out-of-town work? Did you go on the road much? Not very much, Charlie. I was always more or less a homebody guy who couldn't get out of town very much. I went over to the Gulf Coast once when, oh, I forget the name of the play, I believe it was the Hotel Markham. I don't know if that hotel is still in existence. I think it is, yeah. And they had a little band over there. Eddie Miller sent for me. He was playing over there. I went over there, stayed over there about a week, and got so homesick, I said, Eddie, I can't stand this old way. I said, I want to go back to New Orleans.
